question.prompt:
How many ordered pairs of real numbers \((x, y)\) satisfy the following system of equations?

\[ x + 3y = 3 \] \[ \big|\,|x| - |y|\,\big| = 1 \]

solutions.title: Solve four linear cases
solutions.explanation:
The nested absolute value simplifies according to the signs of \(x\) and \(y\). If \(xy\ge0\), then
\[
\bigl||x|-|y|\bigr|=|x-y|;
\]
if \(xy<0\), it equals \(|x+y|\). Therefore every solution must satisfy one of
\[
x=y+1,\quad x=y-1,\quad x=-y+1,\quad x=-y-1.
\]
Substitute each possibility into \(x+3y=3\):

- If \(x=y+1\), then \(4y+1=3\), so \((x,y)=(\tfrac32,\tfrac12)\).
- If \(x=y-1\), then \(4y-1=3\), so \((x,y)=(0,1)\).
- If \(x=-y+1\), then \(2y+1=3\), again giving \((x,y)=(0,1)\).
- If \(x=-y-1\), then \(2y-1=3\), so \((x,y)=(-3,2)\).

These cases cover every possible solution. The three distinct candidates all satisfy the absolute-value equation, since its left side is respectively
\[
\left|\frac32-\frac12\right|=1,\qquad
|0-1|=1,\qquad
|3-2|=1.
\]
The pair \((0,1)\) is counted only once. Thus there are \(\boxed{3}\) ordered pairs, choice \(\text{C}\).
